newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: FEATURE - Korean drivers learn to pump their own gas.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Korean drivers learn to pump their own gas.

text.p: From mini-skirted pump attendants on roller blades to eye-popping decor, South Korean petrol stations go to great lengths to snag a customer.
But the latest development has come as a surprise -- self-service pumps.
In a sign of economic hard times, petrol stations are trying to trim costs, and pampered customers are happy to see those savings translated into cheaper prices.
Stations are still painted in lurid technicolour and the rock music still blares, but the girls who pump petrol, scrub windows and empty ashtrays may be on the way out.
PENNY-PINCHING BACK IN FASHION
So far the self-service experiment is confined to just a handful of stations in Seoul. But oil companies plan to expand the scheme nationwide if it works.
"Ordinary citizens like me need all the savings we can get," said businessman Suh Dong-soo, fumbling with a hose and nozzle at one Seoul station. "Petrol prices are no joke."
Bae Hong-sung, a church pastor, said he had used a self-service pump five times in less than two weeks. "I can save over 1,000 won ($1.12) each time," he said.
Such sentiment is rare among younger South Korean consumers who have abandoned the penny-pinching ways of the post-war generation.

Among the newly affluent young, it is almost a point of honour to pay a premium for goods and services. But times are changing, and oil firms have had to respond as customers shop around to shave a bit off their fuel bills.
TAKING THE EXPERIMENT NATIONWIDE
Consumer spending is slumping across the board during an economic downturn that some analysts describe as the worst in a decade.

Economic growth is forecast at less than six percent this year, down from seven percent last year. Growth is brisk by Western standards but the equivalent of a recession in the minds of many Koreans used to double-digit expansion.

Hyundai Oil Refinery Co is leading the self-service revolution, which started a few weeks ago as part of a price war among oil companies. The nation's oil giants were freed from price controls on January 1.
"We are getting very positive feedback," said Hyundai spokesman Yang Jin-hyung. "We plan to expand the number of self-service stations nationwide."
Hyundai self-service stations offer a discount of 30 won per litre.
"This will be the new trend," said Lee Chul-soo, director of Hyundai Oil Sales Co Ltd. "We will place self-service pumps at six major cities starting in May."
Industry analysts said Hyundai's move was well-timed.
"Customers faced with economic hardship and a higher cost of living will react positively," said Lee Sang-koo, an energy analyst at Hyundai Securities.
Yukong Ltd, the nation's largest oil company, pioneered the self-service pump back in 1992.
"It didn't work," said Yukong spokesman Kim Jeong-ki. "Petrol was cheap then and nobody cared much about getting a discount." An initial 10 self-service stations were scaled back to just two.
"But self-service stations are now gaining popularity," said Kim.
DIRTY HANDS PUT SOME PEOPLE OFF
Not everyone is convinced.
"I don't think it's going to work. Korean pumps are difficult to use, and petrol is still perceived to be dirty and stinky," said Bill Hunsaker, an energy analyst at ING-Baring Securities.
Kang Young-eun, for one, has no intention of soiling her hands to save a few coins -- even though Hyundai thoughtfully supplies white gloves for its patrons.
"I don't want to bother to get out of my car to get petrol," said the Dongduk Woman's University professor. "It's too troublesome. And besides, I don't know how to use the machines."
